definition: Lexical choice is the subtask of Natural language generation that involves choosing the content words (nouns, non-auxiliary verbs, adjectives, and adverbs) in a generated text.
details: Function words (determiners, for example) are usually chosen during realisation.

explainer.lead: Lexical choice is the natural language generation subtask of picking the content words — nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs — that a generated text will use. It matters because word selection shapes meaning and tone before the sentence is fully realised.

tiers.eli5: It is choosing which bricks to use before building the sentence, while the small connecting pieces are slotted in later.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers separate content-word selection from surface realisation so a generator can pick vocabulary from a lexicon and let a realiser handle determiners and agreement. A pitfall is that choices made in isolation can clash with later realisation constraints.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as the NLG subtask selecting content words (nouns, non-auxiliary verbs, adjectives, adverbs); function words such as determiners are typically chosen during realisation. The boundary between the two stages is a design convention rather than a hard rule.

explainer.example: A weather-report generator first chooses the content words 'heavy' and 'rain', then the realiser supplies 'There was heavy rain.'
